overview: This two-page Department of State “List of Papers,” dated October 17, 1945, inventories records filed under the political affairs of Formosa (Taiwan), chiefly from 1931 to 1940. The listed materials concern the suppression of the Taiwan Minshuto, Indigenous resistance and intertribal violence, reactions in Taiwan to Sino-Japanese conflict, provincial administration, press censorship, an alleged Taiwanese Chinese revolt, Japanese expansion and the strategic development of Takao, and the kōminka campaign to assimilate Taiwan’s population into imperial Japanese culture. The list also records cross-references to files on narcotics, the Sino-Japanese conflict, and Japan’s “Southward Advance,” as well as the Department’s favorable assessment of John K. Emmerson’s report on Japanization.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on the political affairs of Formosa
subfiles.about: An index summarizes papers numbered 12–27 concerning political, administrative, ethnic, and strategic developments in Japanese-ruled Taiwan from 1931 through 1940.
subfiles.summary: The first page lists papers on the enforced dissolution of the Taiwan Minshuto, disturbances and violence in Taiwan’s Indigenous regions, an attack on Japanese police, and anxiety among Chinese residents during the Sino-Japanese crisis. The continuation records reports on administrative conferences, restrictions on political news, travel, an alleged Taiwanese Chinese revolt, Taiwan’s role in Japanese expansion, and political repercussions of the conflict in China. It concludes with John K. Emmerson’s report on kōminka, or Japanization, and internal notes stating that the Department rated the report “EXCELLENT” and wished Emmerson to be informed.

interest: The index is valuable as a compact map of how the State Department organized reporting on colonial Taiwan and what American officials considered politically significant. It connects Indigenous resistance, opium politics, censorship, Chinese nationalism, strategic expansion, and cultural assimilation within a single archival sequence. Particularly useful are the references to otherwise dispersed files and the explicit departmental judgment that Emmerson’s report on kōminka was excellent, which reveals both the circulation and contemporary evaluation of diplomatic intelligence.
